To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the liver has a sufficient capacity to detoxify the reactive metabolite(s) of adriamycin, and that this is a primary reason for the relative insensitivity to adriamycin of the liver compared to other tissues, particularly the heart, following acute intoxication.

adriamycin toxicity is mediated by the generation of reactive oxygen species, that the toxicity of adriamycin is not due to a decrease in hepatic glutathione or NADPH, and that species and tissue differences in the distribution and activity of antioxidant defense mechanisms can explain the selective cardiomyopathy of adriamyc in.

the liver is able to maintain a normal redox homeostatic state after adriamycin treatment in the rat, and that species- and/or tissue-specific differences in antioxidant mechanisms may be primary factors in the differential toxicity of adriamycin.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the elucidation of the biochemical mechanisms of adriamycin toxicity.
the role of free radicals in the toxicity of adriamycin and the potential for antioxidant therapy to protect the heart from this toxic effect.
the elucidation of the biochemical basis for the selective toxicity of adriamycin.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, in contrast to the liver, the cardiomyopathy resulting following adriamycin toxicity is not due to a lack of antioxidant defense mechanisms in this tissue.
adriamycin toxicity is not a consequence of a decrease in GSSG-reducing capacity or NADH content.
the toxicity of adriamycin is not related to its ability to generate reactive oxygen species.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the toxicity of adriamycin is due to the formation of reactive oxygen species and that the antioxidant defense systems of the heart are less efficient than those of the liver.
the liver is able to maintain a normal redox homeostatic state following adriamycin treatment.
adriamycin toxicity results primarily from the consumption of vital reducing equivalents by the reductive activation of the quinonoid drug and not by the subsequent formation of oxygen free radicals.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the liver, in contrast to the heart, is well protected against the generation of reactive intermediates by virtue of the presence of an adequate supply of reducing equivalents and a large GSH pool.
the liver is a relatively insensitive organ to acute adriamycine toxicity, and that the primary site of injury following adriamycin exposure is the heart.
, in the liver, there is sufficient antioxidant protection to maintain GSH homeostasis and to prevent the depletion of NAD.
